item.title: Embedding Voice in the Political Economy
item.content:encoded:
Sean O'Brady, McMaster University

Katherine Ravenswood, Auckland University of Technology

Tony Dundon, University of Limerick

Trine P. Larsen, University of Warwick

This special issue examines how employee voice functions within power structures and broader political economic systems. While voice has traditionally been studied as feedback and dialogue, the editors argue that insufficient attention has been paid to how voice relates to systemic inequalities, contemporary transformations like digitalisation and climate transitions, and shifting distributions of actor power. The call seeks critical, interdisciplinary research that theorizes voice as fundamentally embedded in political economic relations rather than treating external contexts as background factors.

Appel publié par British Journal of Industrial Relations. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

item.title: Reconfiguring the Global Politics of Care: Actors, Transformations and Policy Alternatives
item.content:encoded:
Elifcan Celebi, University of Oxford

Rossella Ciccia,

Ayşe Dursun, University of Vienna

David Palomera, University of Southern Denmark

The global care sector faces intensifying challenges from demographic changes, the pandemic, and fiscal constraints, resulting in overburdened systems and widening inequalities. Market-based and government responses have increasingly transformed care through commodification, financialisation, digitalization, and platformisation, with varied consequences across different regions and economies.

This special issue seeks empirical research exploring how care governance is being reshaped by economic, social, and technological changes, and how new political movements are mobilizing around care issues. The editors welcome studies using diverse methodologies and approaches—including feminist, intersectional, and postcolonial perspectives—that examine actors driving these transformations, institutional alternatives emerging across geographies, and policy innovations that might address the care crisis.

Appel publié par Gender Work and Organization. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do ongoing processes of commodification, financialisation, digitalization and (in)formalisation transform care? What roles do markets and financial actors, as well as international organizations, governments, feminist movements, labour organisations, play?
  • How are new and old actors (such as care workers, social movements, care platforms, cooperatives, financial organisations, or public–private and public-communitarian partnerships) reshaping care infrastructures, practices, and labour across the Global North and Global South?
  • How are emerging social, economic and technological processes reconfiguring the relationship between states, markets, families, and communities in different contexts? How do gender, race, care, labour, and migration regimes become entangled in new or altered ways at global, national and local scales? And how do these processes affect gender, class, race, nation hierarchies and intersecting inequalities across caregivers and care receivers?
  • What kind of policy innovations offer promising alternatives to the structural crisis of care? Which proposals in diverse geographies (e.g., communitarian services, caring cities or care commons) from social movements, international organizations, experts, or local initiatives show promise to offer a pathway to a more caring society?

Timeline

  • April 1, 2026: Submissions open
  • October 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Anti-Environmentalism and the Future of Green Growth
item.content:encoded:
Luca Gori, University of Pisa

Simone Marsiglio, University of Pisa

Anastasios Xepapadeas, Athens University of Economics and Business

This special issue addresses the growing political and social opposition to environmental regulation and climate mitigation efforts, examining how anti-environmentalism affects green growth and sustainable development. The collection investigates the drivers and implications of anti-environmental attitudes, considering how economic incentives, institutional factors, and policy design interact with public resistance to environmental policies.

The special issue welcomes research from environmental economics, macroeconomics, political economy, and behavioral economics that explores the relationship between anti-environmentalism and sustainable growth. It seeks comprehensive analysis of mechanisms through which opposition to environmental policies operates and how economic systems can progress toward green growth despite political polarization and societal backlash.

The collection prioritizes methodological contributions—theoretical, empirical, or experimental—that illuminate the complex interactions between anti-environmental movements and green growth. Both participants and non-participants of the related HEDGE conference are encouraged to submit high-quality papers on these topics.

Appel publié par Environmental and Resource Economics. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Economic, social and political determinants of anti-environmental attitudes and behavior
  • Impact of populism, misinformation, and lobbying on climate and environmental policy
  • Public perception and resistance to carbon taxation, green industrial policies, and regulation
  • Distributional and equity aspects of green growth as sources of policy backlash
  • Role of institutions and governance in shaping environmental resistance
  • International and comparative analyses of anti-environmental movements and climate cooperation
  • Behavioral and cultural dimensions of environmental skepticism and pro-growth narratives
  • Policy strategies for overcoming anti-environmentalist sentiment and fostering green transitions
  • Economic growth under climate-related extreme event risk and costs of climate skepticism

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Electoral Competition, Voting, Political Violence, and Policy Outcomes
item.content:encoded:
This special issue of The Quarterly Review of Economics and Finance focuses on the intersection of economics and politics, examining how electoral competition, voting mechanisms, political violence, and policy outcomes interact to shape economic and political systems.
